title: The one who, the thing that
goal: Use *yang* to describe and identify people and things: *orang yang tinggal di sebelah*, *helm yang saya taruh di rak*, and on its own as “the one”: *yang biru, yang mana?, yang penting*.
bekal: describe a lost object precisely: *helm yang biru tua, yang kacanya bening*
ask and answer *Yang mana?* in a shop and choose *yang ini*, not *yang itu*
compare with *yang lebih mahal* and *yang paling murah*

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Helm yang hilang
dialogs.intro: Lunchtime at the office. The blue helmet Mas Bayu lent Sarah, so that she can ride pillion with him to meetings, is no longer on the rack by the entrance. She goes to ask Pak Joko, the security guard (*satpam*).

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Permisi, Pak Joko. Bapak lihat helm yang saya taruh di rak tadi pagi?
lines.id: Excuse me, Pak Joko. Have you seen the helmet I put on the rack this morning?
lines.literal: excuse-me, Mr Joko. you see helmet that I put at rack earlier morning?

lines.speaker: Joko:
lines.text: Helm yang mana, Mbak? Di sini helmnya banyak.
lines.id: Which helmet, Mbak? There are lots of helmets here.
lines.literal: helmet that which, Miss? at here helmet-the many.

lines.text: Yang warna biru tua, ada stiker kucing di belakang.
lines.id: The dark blue one, with a cat sticker on the back.
lines.literal: the-one colour blue old, exist sticker cat at back.

lines.text: Yang kacanya hitam itu?
lines.id: The one with the black visor?
lines.literal: the-one glass-its black that?

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Bukan, kacanya bening. Sebenarnya itu bukan helm saya, tapi punya Mas Bayu.
lines.id: No, the visor's clear. Actually it's not my helmet, it's Mas Bayu's.
lines.literal: not, glass-its clear. actually that not helmet my, but belong Brother Bayu.

lines.text: Laki-laki yang tinggi, rambutnya gondrong, pakai kemeja batik.

lines.text: Tinggi, gondrong, batik… Itu kan Mas Bayu sendiri!

lines.text: Mas, helm yang Mas pinjamkan ke saya hilang dari rak.
lines.id: Bayu, the helmet you lent me has gone from the rack.
lines.literal: Brother, helmet that Brother lend to me lost from rack.

lines.speaker: Bayu:
lines.text: Oh, yang biru? Tadi saya pakai buat beli makan siang. Saya kira Mbak nggak butuh.
lines.id: Oh, the blue one? I wore it to go and get lunch. I thought you didn't need it.
lines.literal: oh, the-one blue? earlier I use for buy eat noon. I think Miss not need.

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Mas! Yang pinjam kan saya. Saya sudah cari dari tadi.
lines.id: Bayu! I'm the one who borrowed it. I've been looking for it for ages.

lines.speaker: Bayu:
lines.text: Maaf, maaf. Yang penting helmnya aman, kan?
lines.id: Sorry, sorry. The main thing is the helmet's safe, right?
lines.literal: sorry, sorry. the-thing-that important helmet-the safe, [kan]?

notes: **Taruh, tadi pagi.** 💬 *Taruh* is the everyday form of *menaruh*, “to put, to leave (somewhere)”. *Tadi* means “earlier today”, so *tadi pagi* is “this morning” when it is already afternoon. For a morning that is still going on you say *pagi ini*.
**Helm yang mana?** “Which one?” in Indonesian is almost always *yang mana*, with or without the noun in front. The answer comes back in the same shape: *yang biru*, *yang ini*, *yang di pojok*.

**Yang warna biru tua.** Once everybody knows you are talking about helmets, *yang* stands in for the noun: “the dark-blue one”. Colours take *tua* (old) for dark and *muda* (young) for light: *biru tua*, *hijau muda*. *Warna* is optional: *yang biru tua* is just as good.
**Punya Mas Bayu.** 💬 *Punya* before a person means “belonging to”: *Ini punya siapa?* — whose is this? The standard written form is *milik*: *helm milik Mas Bayu*.

**Gondrong** is long hair on a man, a word with a faint whiff of the artist or the rebel about it; for a woman's long hair you just say *rambutnya panjang*. *Kok kelihatan panik?* — *kelihatan* is “to look, appear”, and *kok* signals surprise.

**Yang pinjam kan saya.** Putting *yang* + verb first makes the person the focus: “the one who borrowed it is me”. The *kan* adds “as you well know”. *Yang penting…* at the end is the standard way to wrap up a mess: “the main thing is…”.

grammars.title: yang: the one who, the thing that
body: *Yang* links a noun to a description that follows it. The description can be a verb, an adjective or a whole clause; *yang* never changes, whether it means “who”, “which” or “that”.

head: Noun
yang + description
English
rows: the person who lives next door
the person who took the blue helmet
the helmet (that) I put on the rack
the helmet Mas Bayu usually wears

after: Look at the last three rows: when the noun is the *object* of the verb, the clause uses the object-focus shape from Unit 4 (*yang saya taruh*) or a *di-* passive (*yang dipakai*). ⚠️ Not *helm yang saya menaruh*: the *me-* goes as soon as the person comes before the verb.
With one simple adjective you usually don't need *yang*: *laki-laki tinggi* is a tall man. Adding *yang* picks him out from the others — *laki-laki yang tinggi*, the tall one, not the short one.

grammars.title: yang on its own
body: Leave out the noun and *yang* means “the one (that)”. This is one of the most useful little patterns in the language, especially in shops.

head: Indonesian
English
rows: Is there one in size M?
I'm the one who borrowed it.
The main thing is that it's safe.

after: ⚠️ *Yang* is not a question word. “Who took it?” is *Siapa yang mengambil?* — *siapa* asks, and *yang* links. Learners who say *Yang mengambil?* get a puzzled look.
*Ada yang…?* is the polite shop question for anything: *Ada yang lebih kecil?* (Do you have a smaller one?), *Ada yang warna lain?* (Any other colours?).

dialogs.title: Second dialogue — Memilih batik
dialogs.intro: Saturday. Every Friday is batik day at the office, and Sarah owns exactly one batik shirt. Bu Endang takes her to a batik shop on the ground floor of Pasar Beringharjo.

lines.text: Cari yang mana, Mbak? Kemeja, kain, atau daster?

lines.text: Yang lengan panjang atau yang lengan pendek?

lines.text: Yang lengan panjang. Motif yang ini namanya apa?

lines.text: Itu parang, Mbak. Yang cokelat itu kawung, motif klasik Yogya.
lines.id: That's parang. The brown one is kawung, a classic Yogya pattern.
lines.literal: that parang, Miss. the-one brown that kawung, pattern classic Yogya.

lines.speaker: Endang:
lines.text: Mbak Sarah cocok pakai yang warnanya cerah.
lines.id: Bright colours suit you, Mbak Sarah.

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Yang biru muda itu, Bu? Ada yang ukuran M?
lines.id: That light blue one? Is there one in M?
lines.literal: the-one blue young that, Mrs? exist the-one size M?

lines.speaker: Penjual:
lines.text: Ada, Mbak. Yang ini batik tulis, yang itu batik cap. Yang tulis lebih mahal.
lines.id: Yes. This one is hand-drawn batik, that one is stamped. The hand-drawn one is more expensive.
lines.literal: exist, Miss. the-one this batik write, the-one that batik stamp. the-one write more expensive.

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Kenapa yang tulis lebih mahal?
lines.id: Why is the hand-drawn one more expensive?
lines.literal: why the-one write more expensive?

lines.speaker: Penjual:
lines.text: Karena dibuat dengan tangan, Mbak. Satu kain bisa dua bulan.
lines.id: Because it's made by hand. One piece of cloth can take two months.
lines.literal: because is-made with hand, Miss. one cloth can two month.

lines.speaker: Endang:
lines.text: Ambil yang cap saja, Mbak. Yang penting cantik.
lines.id: Take the stamped one. What matters is that it looks nice.
lines.literal: take the-one stamp just, Miss. the-thing important pretty.

notes: **Cari yang mana?** The shopkeeper's opener, short for *Mau cari yang mana?*. In Beringharjo you will hear it called out from every stall, together with *Monggo, Mbak, dilihat dulu* — please, have a look.

**Lengan panjang** — long-sleeved. For the office and for formal events, men's batik shirts are long-sleeved; short sleeves are for everyday. For women the rules are looser, but long sleeves always look smarter.

**Parang, kawung.** *Parang* is the diagonal wave-like band, *kawung* the pattern of four ovals arranged like a flower, said to come from the palm fruit. Both are classics of the Yogyakarta and Surakarta courts, and every motif has a name and a story.

**Batik tulis, batik cap.** *Tulis* (“written”) batik is drawn in hot wax by hand with a small copper pen, the *canting*; *cap* batik is stamped with a copper block. Cloth that is only printed with a batik pattern is called *kain motif batik* or *printing*, and it is not considered true batik.

**Ada yang ukuran M?** *Ada yang…?* asks whether there is one with a certain quality. You can answer it in one word: *Ada* or *Habis* (sold out). *Ukuran* (size) comes from *ukur*, to measure, plus *-an* — the result of measuring, as in Unit 9.

**Yang penting cantik.** Bu Endang's shopping philosophy in three words. *Cantik* is “pretty, beautiful” for women and things; for men the word is *ganteng*. *Ambil yang cap saja* — the *saja* makes it friendly advice rather than an order.

grammars.title: Comparing with yang lebih and yang paling
body: *Lebih* makes “more”, *paling* makes “most”. With *yang* in front they pick out one item from the others: “the more expensive one”, “the cheapest one”.

head: Indonesian
English
rows: The hand-drawn one is more expensive.
*Yang cap lebih murah daripada yang tulis.*
The stamped one is cheaper than the hand-drawn one.
*Ini batik yang paling mahal di toko ini.*
This is the most expensive batik in this shop.

after: “Than” is *daripada* or, in speech, just *dari*: 💬 *Yang cap lebih murah dari yang tulis.* Indonesians argue about whether *dari* is correct here; in writing, use *daripada*.
*Termahal, termurah* — *ter-* on an adjective is a formal superlative that means the same as *paling*: *batik termahal*. You will see it in advertisements more than you will hear it.

blocks.text: Describing something to a satpam, a shop assistant or a lost-property office is mostly a list of *yang* phrases and *-nya* phrases. These frames cover nearly everything.

head: What
Indonesian
English

It's got a wallet and bike keys in it.
the one I put on the rack

blocks.title: Batik words
items: *batik tulis* hand-drawn in wax; *batik cap* stamped; *kain motif batik* printed pattern
*kain* a length of cloth; *selendang* a scarf or shawl; *daster* a loose house dress
*motif* pattern: *parang, kawung, truntum, sidomukti*
*Hari Batik Nasional* is 2 October; many offices and all government staff wear batik on Fridays

blocks.text: A handful of *yang* phrases are so common that they work almost like single words. Learn them as chunks.
*Yang bener aja* is spoken Jakarta for *yang benar saja* — literally “just the true one!” — and it is what you say when a price or a request is outrageous. Use it with friends, not with Mbak Nur.
Cover the Indonesian column, read the English, and rebuild each sentence from memory.

Get some cakes for Dimas while we're here. He loves market snacks.
*Sekalian beli kue buat Dimas, Mbak. Dia suka jajanan pasar.*
Mbak Sarah, help me, please. I've got homework from my teacher.
*Mbak Sarah, bantuin aku, dong. Aku ada tugas dari Bu Guru.*
Fine. But cut slowly — don't catch your hand with the scissors.
*Boleh. Tapi motongnya pelan-pelan, jangan sampai tanganmu kena gunting.*
